title: Command Lookup and Execution knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Command Lookup and Execution”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Executable files” under lesson 14, “Command Lookup and Execution”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Command Lookup and Execution”?
options: Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Use commands and arguments deliberately, and inspect stdout, stderr, and the exit status separately.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
questions.answer_key: Use commands and arguments deliberately, and inspect stdout, stderr, and the exit status separately.
questions.explanation: Use commands and arguments deliberately, and inspect stdout, stderr, and the exit status separately. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Command Lookup and Execution”?
options: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
questions.answer_key: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
questions.explanation: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
